title: Carbon emissions are down this year—but that probably won’t last
gist: A Global Carbon Project analysis led by Corinne Le Quéré estimates 2026 fossil CO2 emissions fell about 0.4%, driven mainly by an Iran-war oil price shock rather than structural decline; EVs, solar and wind covered nearly 70% of energy demand growth. Extrapolating IMF GDP projections, emissions should resume rising, with a sustained peak possibly a few years away.

insights.claim: Global fossil fuel CO2 emissions are estimated to fall about 0.4 percent in 2026, versus a 1.2 percent rise in 2025 and a 2019-2025 average increase of 0.8 percent per year, according to a Global Carbon Project analysis led by Corinne Le Quéré.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: A headline emissions decline that researchers attribute to a temporary shock, not a peak.
insights.locator: A new analysis led by Corinne Le Quéré

insights.claim: The 2026 emissions dip is attributed mainly to high oil prices from the war in Iran: oil emissions fell 1.9 percent, natural gas 0.3 percent, while coal emissions rose 0.6 percent.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Price-driven oil demand destruction is real but reversible once prices normalize; coal kept growing.
insights.locator: Last year, fossil fuel emissions increased 1.2 percent

insights.claim: Electric vehicles account for only about 20 percent of the 2026 decline in oil emissions, meaning most of the drop came from high prices rather than structural substitution.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Oil demand should rebound if Iran-related price pressure eases.

insights.claim: Unlike the 2020 pandemic drop, 2026 energy demand rose, but additions of electric vehicles, solar and wind covered almost 70 percent of the demand growth.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Clean tech is now absorbing most incremental energy demand — supportive for renewables and EV volumes.

insights.claim: Between 2019 and 2025, 59 countries cut emissions despite economic growth, and without EV, solar and wind growth global emissions would have risen 1.9 percent per year instead of 0.8 percent.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Quantifies clean tech's impact: it more than halved emissions growth.
insights.locator: Between 2019 and 2025, 59 countries cut their emissions

insights.claim: Extrapolating trends with IMF GDP projections through 2028 implies global fossil emissions will keep rising; without the oil price shock, 2026 emissions would also have increased.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Do not treat 2026 as peak emissions; fossil demand growth likely resumes.
insights.locator: Given the International Monetary Fund's projection

insights.claim: Researchers say a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away if clean technology deployment keeps accelerating, since current growth offsets most but not all emissions growth.
insights.speaker: Scott K. Johnson
insights.so_what: Peak emissions timing depends on continued clean-tech acceleration — a policy-sensitive variable for energy transition investments.
insights.quote: If further acceleration of clean technology deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away.
insights.locator: So while we could be close to peak emissions
